header: Date: 2026-05-01 15:00 UTC | Duration: 40m | Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE); Maya Chen (Redwood SE); Priya Rao (Nova Head of ML); David Kim (Nova Infra); Lena Ortiz (Nova Product); Aaron Bell (Nova CTO)
summary: Discovery focused on Nova's latency and throughput requirements for an LLM-powered feature. Primary concerns: p95 latency targets (<=150ms for short completions, <=500ms for streaming long responses), concurrency and burst patterns, token/sec benchmarking, and data residency/security for pilot. AE + SE committed to share pricing, SOC2/ISO docs, and a benchmark plan; customer to provide traffic profile and sample prompts for a dedicated capacity pilot.
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Samir from Redwood, that's Maya our solutions engineer — thanks for taking the time. how's everyone doing?
[00:10] Priya: Good thanks yeah excited to talk through this, lots of context to share.
[00:15] Samir: Great, quick agenda. we want to understand your latency p95 targets, typical concurrency, streaming needs, and any security constraints so we can recommend hosted vs dedicated vs private. sound good?
[00:26] Aaron: Yup. and we also want to see what latencies we can realistically expect at scale, like p95 and p99 and tokens per second numbers.
[00:32] Maya: Perfect. can you give us a quick rundown of the feature you're building and the expected traffic profile?
[00:38] Priya: Sure. We're adding an in-product assistant that helps analysts summarize datasets and run ad-hoc queries. Short prompts are common — e.g., "summarize last 7 days" — which are ~20-60 tokens, and longer streaming completions for step-by-step guided analysis that can be 800-2k tokens.
[00:53] Priya: Concurrency: baseline 150 concurrent users during peak with spiky bursts up to 800 concurrent for short windows (a few minutes) when batch jobs hit. Latency target: p95 for short completions needs to be <=150ms ideally, though <=250ms is acceptable. For streaming long responses we want p95 end-to-end under 500ms for first token and steady streaming thereafter.
[01:16] David: infra constraints: we're on AWS, multi-region US-east and EU-west. data residency matters for EU customers. we also need SSO/SAML, audit logs, and KMS integration for keys.
[01:26] Maya: Thanks — that's helpful. just to clarify, when you say p95 <=150ms for short completions, is that end-to-end including network and your app layer?
[01:34] Priya: Yes, that's from user click to first meaningful token shown in UI. we can tolerate slightly higher for longer completions.
[01:41] Samir: Got it. a few quick notes on Redwood model tiers: Hosted gives fastest onboarding, predictable per-token pricing, and autoscaling but shared infra — good for getting started. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools, predictable latency at scale and isolation; Private (VPC/on-prem) is for strict residency and compliance.
[01:58] Aaron: For p95 <150ms, do you have public benchmarks or examples? we saw some numbers on your docs but want realistic numbers for our workload.
[02:06] Maya: We do — and it depends a lot on model size, sequence length, and batching. For short sequences (<=64 tokens) on quantized Llama2/Redwood-optimized models in Dedicated, we routinely see p95 around 80-140ms at moderate concurrency, but it varies with batching and your request pattern.
[02:24] David: What about token/sec throughput? if we have 800 concurrent short requests, what's tokens/sec and token costs look like?
[02:30] Maya: Two axes: tokens/sec per GPU (affected by model and precision) and requests/sec considering batching. Example: a T4-style GPU at 8-bit quant might do X tokens/sec — (note: placeholder numbers in call) — but in Dedicated on A100 or H100 we often benchmark 10k-40k tokens/sec per GPU depending on model and optimizations. for short requests, it's more about requests/sec and latency SLOs than raw tokens/sec.
[02:52] Priya: Okay that's helpful. could you talk about streaming first-token latency versus full-completion latency? we need the assistant to be perceived as snappy.
[02:59] Maya: Yes, streaming first-token latency is influenced by model compilation, cold KV cache misses, and routing. With warm caches and reserved capacity, first-token p95 for streaming on medium models is often <200-300ms. We also do prefix/KV caching to speed up repeated prompts.
[03:16] Priya: You mentioned KV cache — our prompts are often similar with shared prefixes, so caching could help. what's the cache hit rate you typically see?
[03:22] Maya: Hit rate varies; teams with templated prompts often see >60% prefix cache hits which drops token costs and latency significantly. we can instrument that in the pilot.
[03:30] Samir: Quick question for David — are you planning to use the hosted API during pilot or go straight to Dedicated?
[03:35] David: We want to evaluate hosted first to move quickly, but if latency at scale isn't there we'll look at Dedicated. also because of EU-residency we might need dedicated or private for EU customers.
[03:45] Samir: Makes sense. we'll propose a two-phase approach: quick hosted POC for integration and functional testing; run dedicated capacity benchmark to validate latency under your concurrency.
[03:54] Lena: On the cost side, how much does Dedicated typically cost compared to hosted? ballpark is fine.
[03:59] Samir: Ballpark: hosted is pay-as-you-go per token; dedicated is a reserved capacity commit which gives substantially lower unit costs for heavy steady traffic. we'll send a SKU-level pricing sheet — it'll show per-token equivalent at different commit tiers.
[04:12] Aaron: For benchmarking — we'd like to run tokens/sec tests plus request patterns that emulate 150 baseline with spikes to 800. what tooling do you recommend?
[04:20] Maya: We'll provide a benchmark plan and scripts. typical approach: 1) synthetic load testing with JMeter/Locust against the Redwood API to simulate request mix; 2) run real prompt sample against model variants to measure p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec; 3) run streaming trials to capture first-token latency and steady-state throughput.
[04:40] Priya: Can you also include step-by-step instructions and any client-side timing hooks we should add to measure true end-to-end?
[04:45] Maya: Absolutely — we'll include a timing snippet you can drop in UI to measure click-to-first-token, and guidance on accounting for network.
[04:52] David: A couple technical constraints: our user base is global, and we want region-aware routing to keep EU traffic in EU datacenters; do you support region routing and fallbacks?
[05:01] Samir: Yes, region routing is supported. Powered by smart routing policies — we can pin EU customers to EU-hosted/dedicated capacity and fallback to other regions with a policy. We'll share doc links.
[05:10] Aaron: For Dedicated — what's the typical provisioning lead time?
[05:13] Maya: Depends on instance type and availability; for standard reserved GPU pools it's usually a few days to a couple weeks. if it's an on-prem private install, that's longer (coordination with infra/ops).
[05:22] Priya: Let's talk SLOs — do you have SLA-backed p95 numbers?
[05:26] Samir: We offer SLAs for Dedicated on availability and throughput commitments; latency SLOs are part of the operational contract and can be negotiated for larger commits.
[05:35] David: Any risks around cold-starts or model load/unload affecting p95?
[05:39] Maya: Cold starts can impact first few requests if the model isn't resident. We mitigate with pinned model instances for Dedicated, and pre-warm ops during critical windows. For Hosted, we use warm pools and auto-scale thresholds tuned to minimize cold starts but it's a tradeoff.
[05:53] Priya: If we go with Hosted for the pilot, how do you help with observability to debug latency outliers?
[05:58] Maya: Redwood Console gives per-request tracing, token-level latency breakdowns, KV cache hit metrics, route-level dashboards, and exportable traces. SEs can add tracing hooks to correlate with your app.
[06:10] Aaron: We're also curious about model variants and quantization. If we quantize, how much does that affect quality and latency?
[06:16] Maya: Quantization (8-bit/4-bit) reduces memory and improves tokens/sec and latency, but can have small quality regressions depending on tasks. Redwood Optimize recommends quant profiles per workload and we'll run quality checks during benchmark.
[06:29] Priya: For long streaming responses (1k+ tokens), what's the typical steady-state tokens/sec we can expect?
[06:36] Maya: On high-end GPUs with optimized kernels you'll see thousands of tokens/sec aggregate; per-request steady-state depends on batching and whether you're doing single-request streaming or multiplexed on the same GPU. We'll capture real numbers in the benchmark for your exact model+prompt mix.
[06:55] Samir: Quick aside — do you have an existing model preference (open models vs closed like OpenAI)?
[06:59] Priya: We're leaning open models for cost and control; probably Llama2 variants or similar.
[07:05] Maya: Good — those map well to Redwood's optimized paths. we'll include specific recommendations and expected latencies for common open models.
[07:12] David: On networking, we'll need IP allowlists and a secure peering/VPC setup if we go dedicated. what does that look like?
[07:19] Samir: For Dedicated and Private we support VPC peering and private connectivity, and we can work with your network team to set up IP allowlists, private endpoints, and KMS integration. we'll include a network diagram in the security pack.
[07:29] Lena: For our product team, we care a lot about perceived latency; even if backend times are slightly higher, trickle-first-token UX matters. can you support low-latency first-token then chunked streaming?
[07:38] Maya: Yes, Redwood supports low-latency first-token streaming and chunked token emission. It's configurable — we can tune batch windows and max-latency thresholds to favor first-token performance.
[07:48] Priya: For the benchmark, can we test two modes: aggressive batching (to maximize cost-efficiency) and low-latency single-request mode so we can see tradeoffs?
[07:55] Maya: Absolutely. we'll run both modes: batching-heavy to show ideal cost per token and low-latency single-request to show p95 improvements.
[08:03] David: How do you account for client-side network variance in metrics?
[08:07] Maya: We recommend instrumenting client hooks for click-to-first-token and including a small set of regional agents to generate traffic; our benchmark scripts can simulate network latencies. we also give breakdowns for service-side vs network time.
[08:20] Aaron: Any customer references with similar latency targets?
[08:23] Samir: We can introduce you to a couple of fintech and retail customers who run p95 in this range on Dedicated — i'll loop them in offline.
[08:31] Priya: On authentication, we need SSO + RBAC for team access and audit trails for every inference call.
[08:37] Maya: We support SSO/SAML, RBAC, and per-token audit logs. We'll include the compliance pack.
[08:45] Samir: Great — looks like we're converging. i'll summarize next steps at the end. any remaining technical nitty gritty?
[08:51] David: One thing — for the dedicated pilot, what's the billing model if we overshoot the reserved capacity in test spikes?
[08:57] Samir: Dedicated has burst policies; there are burst credits and overage rates which we'll detail in the pricing sheet. for benchmarking we can provision temporary extra capacity or throttle to emulate limits.
[09:08] Priya: Also please include model quality baseline checks during the benchmark so we can compare quantized vs float.
[09:14] Maya: We'll include eval prompts and automated quality checks; we'll measure output metrics and flag regressions.
[09:22] (brief cross talk)
[09:27] Samir: Okay — i'll read back the agreed next steps: 1) Redwood sends pricing + SKU options and compliance docs, 2) Redwood shares benchmark plan + scripts, 3) Nova shares traffic profile and sample prompts, 4) schedule benchmark window. Anything to add?
[09:45] Priya: Add that we need sample dataset constraints noted — PII constraints, redaction requirements.
[09:49] Samir: Noted. we'll add that to the pilot checklist.
[09:53] Aaron: Cool. thanks everyone.
[09:55] Samir: Thanks — we'll follow up with the packet today.
[10:00] END

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription had a few mis-recognitions (model names like "Redwood-optimized" sometimes transcribed as "red wood"), speaker labels are mostly correct, occasional crosstalk.
notes: AE+SE present; agreed to two-phase pilot: hosted quick POC, then Dedicated benchmark. Customer to provide prompts and traffic profile. Compliance and network docs to be shared.
